lines.caption: Every field in a Rayfin entity gets a decorator. So what does each one actually do?
Watch one line become a database column, and the rules your data has to follow.
Hi, I'm Ray! Welcome back to Learn Rayfin with Ray.
Today: how to write an entity, what each field decorator stores, and how to register it. Let's dive in!
An entity is a class with the entity decorator. Your app keeps each one in its own file, in the data package.

lines.said: Every entity has an ID: a U U I D primary key named id. Leave it out, and Rayfin adds it for you.
lines.caption: Every entity has an ID: a UUID primary key named id. Leave it out, and Rayfin adds it for you.
Every other field you want stored gets exactly one field decorator.
Text holds strings. Int holds whole numbers. Decimal holds exact numbers, like money, with two decimal places by default.

lines.said: Boolean is true or false, date is a date and time, and U U I D holds I D's.
lines.caption: Boolean is true or false, date is a date and time, and uuid holds IDs.
Email is text that has to look like an email address. And set allows only the values you list.
Fields are required by default. To make one optional, set optional to true, and add a question mark. You need both.
Default fills in a value you leave out. Unique stops two records from sharing a value.
Min and max bound a text's length, or a number's range.
A set's values go in the decorator, and again as the property's type.
Rayfin enforces these for you, and can even turn them into a form validator.
Last step: register the entity. Until you do, it doesn't exist as far as your client's concerned.
In the data package's index file, export the class, and add it to the schema list.

lines.said: In the shared package, describe its record, and add it to Universal App Schema: the type your client is checked against.
lines.caption: In the shared package, describe its record, and add it to UniversalAppSchema: the type your client is checked against.
And don't name an entity after a GraphQL type, like Date or Query. The CLI rejects it. Try EventDate instead.
Time for a deep dive! What happens to a text field with no max?
Each field becomes a column in your app's database. Text with a max of two hundred holds up to two hundred characters.
Leave max out, and the column gets the database's maximum length.
On some databases, Rayfin can fail to build your GraphQL schema from a column like that.
Worse, you find out late. rayfin up reports success, then your queries fail with an internal server error.
So give every text a max that fits its data: fifty for a short name, two thousand for a description.
Email, too. It takes the same options as text.
Here's the same idea in Fabricator. Blueprint's Data model view draws each entity as a card: every field, with its type.
A key marks the ID, and a set shows up as enum.
A filled diamond means required. A hollow one means optional, like the note.
And Open takes you to the entity's file, in Code.
Pop quiz! What's wrong with this field?
A, it needs a question mark. B, it has no max. Or C, text can't be required.
Pause the video, and guess…
It's B! With no max, your queries can fail after a deploy that looked fine. Give every text a max.
Let's recap. Each stored field gets one decorator, and its options become rules. Register every entity in the data and shared packages. And give every text a max.
Your challenge: send this prompt in Fabricator, then find your new entity in Blueprint's Data model.
Then tell me in the comments: which decorators did it get?
Next time: relationships, and how Rayfin knows a customer has many orders. See you in the water!
